newsitem.title: UK: New British financial watchdog to involve industry.
newsitem.headline: New British financial watchdog to involve industry.

text.p: Britain's powerful new financial watchdog will continue to consult market practitioners and maintain different levels of regulation for wholesale and retail business, Treasury minister Helen Liddell said on Thursday.

Liddell told a conference organised by the Institute of Economic Affairs work was already in hand to smooth the transition to the Labour government's planned single regulator, merging together the existing watchdogs.
"The UK financial services industry needs a world leader. We must seize the opportunity now to develop a modern regulatory structure to see us through well into the next century," Liddell said.

But while the Super-Securities and Investments Board (SIB) would be a single regulator underpinned by statute with responsibilities across the financial sector, Liddell did not say whether it would encompass insurance, building societies, Lloyd's of London insurance market and recognised professional bodies.

Liddell outlined the stages which would eventually lead to the formation of the new watchdog, which would wrap together the roles played by the "frontline regulators" or self-regulatory organisations (SROs) set up by the Financial Services Act of 1986.

The first step, she said, would be a Bank of England bill. This was likely to be put before parliament after the summer and would transfer responsibility for supervising banks from the Bank of England to the enhanced SIB.
This transfer should take place early in 1998 but in the meantime the Bank of England and SIB were planning "how the merger can take place with minimum disruption".

The next step, Liddell said, would be a bill to reform the regulation of financial services. She acknowledged this would be "long and quite complex" but said the government hoped to publish it in the summer of 1998.
"This bill will pave the way for the integration of the SROs into the enhanced SIB in late 1999 or early 2000," she added.
There was also a warning to the financial services industry if it ignored the government's invitation to help shape the regulatory framework.

"If the industry ignores this opportunity to help shape the new regulatory regime, then they will have no one else to blame but themselves," she said. The goal was not a huge monolith but a clear, visible and accountable structure, she said. Rather than tearing everything up, Liddell planned to build on the existing structure, learning from past mistakes.
The minister also stressed the importance of maintaining quality staff and made a plea for firms to make top people available on secondment.
"It will need people who are knowledgeable and streetwise. This will be no soft option for these staff. SIB can use your smartest and strongest."
She also addressed concerns among several conference delegates that too much emphasis would be on the customer rather than the industry.

"It is the job of government to keep under review the balance between sufficient regulation to maintain public confidence and over-regulation where we lose sight of what it is we are trying to achieve," she said.
